title: The CIA Stole Part of a Soviet Nuclear Sub With a Giant Claw
title_candidates: The CIA Stole Part of a Soviet Nuclear Sub With a Giant Claw
The CIA Built a Fake Mining Ship to Steal a Soviet Nuclear Sub
Howard Hughes's Fake Mining Ship Was a CIA Submarine Heist
blurb: In 1974 the CIA used a fake deep-sea mining ship, sold to the world as Howard Hughes's, to grab a sunken Soviet nuclear submarine from three miles down. Meatball opens the case file on Project Azorian: the submarine that vanished, the claw, the lift that broke in half, and how 'we can neither confirm nor deny' got its name. Every claim is from the CIA's own declassified history, the CIA Museum or the National Security Archive. Confirmed (CIA): the sub, the cover story, the claw, the breakup halfway up, part of the sub recovered, six sailors buried at sea. Disputed or unconfirmed: how much was recovered (a 38-ft bow section per Blind Man's Bluff), two nuclear torpedoes (1993 Russian report), no missiles (Navy officials quoted by the NYT), how the US found the wreck (SOSUS, per 1970s books), the cost (~$500 million estimate). Still classified: what the recovered section held and the cause of the sinking.

beats.say: In nineteen seventy-four, the CIA tried to steal a Soviet nuclear submarine. From three miles under the Pacific. With a giant claw.

shots.photo: CIA painting of the AZORIAN recovery
CIA model of the sunken K-129

beats.say: To hide it, they put a billionaire's name on a ship, Howard Hughes, and told the world it was mining rocks.

shots.photo: Manganese nodule from the cover story (CIA)

beats.say: It half worked. And the answer the CIA gave reporters became the most famous non-answer in government. That one's at the end.
Honestly? I've never stolen anything bigger than a breadstick. This case is way above my pay grade.

shots.photo: CIA model of the sunken K-129

beats.say: Comment your guess before I open the file. How much of the submarine did they actually get? All of it? A piece? Or nothing?

shots.photo: CIA model of the sunken K-129
CIA painting of the AZORIAN recovery

beats.say: I'm Meatball, by the way. I open real case files and tell you what's proven. Subscribe. There's a new case every week.
Number one. The submarine. March, nineteen sixty-eight. A Soviet submarine called K-129 sails out of Petropavlovsk, on Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula.
It's a diesel submarine of the Golf Two class. And it carries three ballistic missiles with nuclear warheads.
Its job: wait quietly in the Pacific, northeast of Hawaii. If war broke out, it could fire those missiles at the American west coast.
Then, in March, it goes silent. It never comes home. Every man aboard is lost.
What sank it? Officially, still unknown. Even the CIA's own history of this case says nothing about the cause.

shots.photo: CIA model of the sunken K-129

beats.say: I lose things all the time. Socks. A fork, once. But a whole submarine? That's a big thing to lose.
Number two. The search. The Soviet navy goes looking for its submarine. They search and search. They can't find it.
Eventually, they give up. But here's the twist. Somebody else was listening.
The United States found it. Exactly how is still officially secret.
Books in the nineteen seventies reported that US Navy underwater microphones had picked up the sound, and narrowed down the spot.
And the spot was deep. Sixteen thousand five hundred feet. That's more than three miles of black, freezing water.

shots.photo: CIA model of the sunken K-129

beats.say: The CIA's own museum describes the job like this. Stand on top of the Empire State Building, holding a grappling hook on a steel rope.

shots.photo: CIA painting of the AZORIAN recovery

beats.say: Lower it all the way to the street. Grab a small car. And lift it back to the top. Without anyone noticing.

shots.photo: CIA painting of the AZORIAN recovery

beats.say: Except the car is a broken submarine, about a hundred and thirty feet long, weighing around seventeen hundred and fifty tons.

shots.photo: CIA model of the sunken K-129

beats.say: I once tried to lift a meatball sub. I dropped it. And I'm basically made of meatball sub.

shots.photo: CIA model of the sunken K-129

beats.say: So why try? Because a Soviet missile submarine meant its missiles, maybe its code books, and secrets about Soviet weapons nobody in America had ever held.
The CIA took the job. And the plan it picked was the strangest one on the table. It gets worse.

shots.photo: CIA painting of the AZORIAN recovery

beats.say: Number three. The cover story. In nineteen sixty-nine, President Nixon approves a special secret team inside the CIA, just for this.
The secret gets locked inside a security code word: Jennifer. Even Henry Kissinger is on the short list of people who know.
Now here's the funny part. For years, books called the whole mission Jennifer. Wrong. That was just the lock. The mission's name was Azorian.

shots.photo: Project AZORIAN artifacts at the CIA Museum

beats.say: And even the people running it thought the odds were terrible. Early on, they gave it about a ten percent chance of working.
You can't hide a ship that big. So they hid it in plain sight. They needed a reason for a giant ship to sit in the middle of the ocean, dangling machinery to the sea floor.
Enter Howard Hughes. The billionaire.
The story: a Hughes company had built a ship to mine the ocean floor, scooping up metal-rich lumps called manganese nodules.

shots.photo: Manganese nodule from the cover story (CIA)

beats.say: This is one of the nodules from the cover story. The CIA kept it, sealed in plastic, in its museum.

shots.photo: Manganese nodule from the cover story (CIA)

beats.say: They even made ship coveralls and ashtrays, so every little detail matched the lie.

shots.photo: Project AZORIAN artifacts at the CIA Museum

beats.say: Branded ashtrays. That's commitment. My cover story is that I'm a regular meatball. Nobody has ever checked.

shots.photo: Project AZORIAN artifacts at the CIA Museum

beats.say: And the public believed it. To the world, this was a mining ship. But it was hiding something in its belly.
Number four. The ship. November, nineteen seventy-one. Workers lay its keel at a shipyard in Chester, Pennsylvania.
It becomes the Hughes Glomar Explorer. A tall derrick in the middle, like an oil rig. Two tall docking legs. A crane just for pipe.
The secret was underneath. A giant well in the middle of the ship, with doors in its floor. They called it the moon pool.

shots.photo: CIA painting of the AZORIAN recovery

beats.say: Open those doors, and the ship could work straight down into the ocean, from inside itself, where no other ship, plane or spy satellite could see.

shots.photo: CIA painting of the AZORIAN recovery

beats.say: And what went down through that pool? The claw. The CIA called it the capture vehicle. Giant steel jaws, built to grab a submarine.

shots.photo: CIA painting of the AZORIAN recovery

beats.say: Even the claw was built in secret, under a roof, then loaded into the ship from a barge sunk underneath it.
A secret ship, with a secret pool, with a secret claw inside. Three secrets, stacked like a sandwich. A sub sandwich.
It almost never sailed. In nineteen seventy-one, the costs ran so high the project nearly got cancelled.
Then in nineteen seventy-two, top Pentagon officials recommended killing it. Too expensive, too risky, and maybe not worth it.
President Nixon overruled them. December, nineteen seventy-two. Keep going.
How much did it all cost? The CIA still hasn't said. Later estimates run to about half a billion dollars, in nineteen seventies money.
If you can't believe this is real, hit like. And stick around. That famous non-answer is still coming.
Now the hard part. Lowering that claw three miles down, while the Soviets watch. Coming up.
Number five. The lift. June, nineteen seventy-four. Nixon approves the mission, but tells them to wait until he's back from a summit in Moscow.
On July fourth, nineteen seventy-four, the Glomar Explorer arrives over the wreck.
To reach the bottom, the crew joins steel pipe sixty feet at a time, and lowers the claw on the end of it. For three miles.

shots.photo: CIA painting of the AZORIAN recovery
CIA model of the sunken K-129

beats.say: Then company arrives. Soviet navy ships show up and start watching. For almost two weeks, they circle the mining ship.
The crew worried the Soviets might land a helicopter and come aboard. So they stacked crates on the helicopter deck.
A team was told to be ready to destroy the secret equipment if anyone boarded. The CIA's history adds: guns were not issued.
I'd have hidden in the moon pool. Meatballs float, right?
August first. The claw closes around the submarine, and the lift begins.

shots.photo: CIA painting of the AZORIAN recovery

beats.say: Slowly. One pipe section at a time. It takes days.

shots.photo: CIA model of the sunken K-129

beats.say: And then, about halfway up, it happens. The submarine breaks apart.

shots.photo: CIA painting of the AZORIAN recovery

beats.say: A big part of it falls back to the bottom of the ocean. Three miles down. Gone.

shots.photo: CIA model of the sunken K-129

beats.say: The crew is crushed. But part of the sub is still in the claw. And they bring it up. On August eighth, it's safe inside the ship.
So what did they actually get? This is where the file goes dark.
Confirmed by the CIA: they raised part of the submarine. And inside were the bodies of six Soviet sailors.

shots.photo: CIA model of the sunken K-129

beats.say: No jokes here. The six men were given a formal military burial at sea, and the CIA filmed it.
In nineteen ninety-two, CIA director Robert Gates handed that film to Russia's president, Boris Yeltsin.
The CIA's history also mentions the crew cleaning up plutonium contamination, from at least one of the sub's nuclear torpedoes.

shots.photo: CIA model of the sunken K-129

beats.say: Disputed: how much they got. A nineteen ninety-eight book, Blind Man's Bluff, reported it was only the front thirty-eight feet of the sub.

shots.photo: CIA model of the sunken K-129
CIA painting of the AZORIAN recovery

beats.say: A Russian report in nineteen ninety-three concluded the CIA got two nuclear torpedoes. The CIA has never confirmed that.
And the big prize, the missiles? In nineteen seventy-five, the New York Times reported Navy officials saying no missiles came up.
What exactly was in that piece? Still classified. Fifty years later, those parts of the file are still blacked out.
So: half a success, kept perfectly secret. Except it wasn't. Remember that answer I promised? It starts with a burglary.
Number six. The leak. June, nineteen seventy-four, just before the ship sailed. Thieves broke into one of Howard Hughes's company offices in Los Angeles.
beats.chapter: The leak: neither confirm nor deny

beats.say: They stole secret documents. And one of them tied Howard Hughes to the CIA, and to the Glomar Explorer.
The CIA was desperate to get it back. It called in the FBI. The FBI called in the Los Angeles police. All for one piece of paper.
Imagine being those burglars. You break into an office, and you walk out holding a Cold War secret.
All that searching drew attention. By the fall, reporters were hearing rumors.
CIA director William Colby personally asked the people who knew not to publish. For a while, they didn't.
Then, on February seventh, nineteen seventy-five, the Los Angeles Times printed it. Hughes. The CIA. A submarine.
In March, columnist Jack Anderson broke it on the air, and the New York Times ran Seymour Hersh's story.

shots.photo: President Ford at the White House (NARA)

beats.say: Reporters flooded Long Beach, where the ship was getting ready for a second try. And the Soviets sent a ship to guard the wreck.
The cover was blown. The White House cancelled the second mission.
Now here's the twist. A journalist named Harriet Ann Phillippi asked the CIA for its records, under the Freedom of Information Act.
The CIA's reply: it could neither confirm nor deny that the records even existed.
She sued. And in nineteen seventy-six, a federal appeals court sided with the CIA.
That answer is now named after the mining ship. It's called a Glomar response. Agencies still use it today.
So the most famous way to say nothing in Washington is named after a ship that was pretending to mine rocks.

shots.photo: Manganese nodule from the cover story (CIA)

beats.say: And the last twist? The cover story came true. After the CIA was done, the ship went on test mining voyages. Later it was rebuilt as a real deep-sea drilling ship.
The fake mining ship ended up actually mining. I respect that. That's a meatball who became a real chef.
So. Did the CIA really build a fake mining ship to steal a Soviet nuclear submarine?

shots.photo: CIA painting of the AZORIAN recovery

beats.say: Yes. In twenty ten, the CIA declassified its own history of Project Azorian. It's all on the record.

shots.photo: Project AZORIAN artifacts at the CIA Museum

beats.say: Did it work? Partly. They got a piece. What was in that piece, they still won't fully say.

shots.photo: CIA model of the sunken K-129
